analysis.one_liner: Caps loan interest rates at whatever limit the borrower's home state allows.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would cap consumer loan rates at each state's maximum, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in June 2023 and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal lending law so that the interest rate on almost any consumer loan — credit cards, installment loans, payday-style loans — could not exceed the maximum rate allowed in the state where the borrower lives, with fees counted toward the cap. Today, many lenders get around state rate limits by partnering with a bank based in a state with no cap. This bill would close that route. It was never taken up by the Senate Banking Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers in states with strict interest rate caps — most states cap rates well below what payday and installment lenders charge — would stop paying triple-digit APRs on loans funneled through out-of-state banks or structured to evade state law. State governments and their attorneys general would regain the power to enforce their own usury laws against national lenders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

how_it_helps.text: It would make any consumer loan's interest rate — including fees folded into the APR — subject to the maximum rate allowed in the borrower's own state, no matter where the lender is chartered.

Because the cap covers 'any consumer credit transaction' other than mortgages, it would reach credit cards, installment loans, and payday-style products that today escape state rate caps through the 'rent-a-bank' arrangement, in which a nationally chartered bank nominally makes the loan and the bank's home state's rules apply.

analysis.who_pays: High-cost lenders — payday, installment, and subprime credit lenders — would lose the ability to charge rates above each borrower's state limit, which in most states would make their lending unprofitable. Some borrowers with poor credit would lose access to the high-priced loans they currently use.

drawbacks.text: A national cap tied to each state's law would cut off access to higher-cost credit for borrowers with poor credit histories who currently use subprime installment loans or payday-style products through bank partnerships; some of these borrowers could lose access to any legal borrowing and turn to unregulated or informal lenders.

The cap applies to virtually all consumer credit except mortgages, so its effect on prices and availability of auto loans, credit cards, and personal loans — not just small-dollar loans — would be large and hard to predict, and lenders could respond with tighter underwriting that screens out the riskiest borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be real but uneven: it would stop high-cost installment and payday lenders from exporting their home state's loose rate limits nationwide, in states that set strict caps. The cost is that some consumers with poor credit who currently borrow at triple-digit rates might lose access to legal credit and turn to worse informal options. The bill never advanced far enough for anyone to test these trade-offs formally.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee never acted on the bill, so it never got a hearing, a vote, or a path to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Whitehouse introduced the bill on June 13, 2023 with four Democratic-affiliated cosponsors (Reed, Warren, Sanders, and Merkley).
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was recorded: the committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and it died at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost consumer lenders — payday, installment, and rent-a-bank lenders — kept the ability to charge rates above many states' caps. Borrowers in states with strict rate limits continue paying whatever the national market charges.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap consumer loan rates at each borrower's home state limit.

for.name: Sens. Jack Reed, Elizabeth Warren, Bernie Sanders, and Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senators signed on.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no report to the full Senate.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's independents; no Republican supported the bill, and the Banking Committee, where it died, was where the bill had no path forward.

industries.industry: High-cost consumer lenders (payday, installment, and subprime credit card lenders)
industries.note: These lenders' business models depend on charging rates above what many states allow, which the bill would bar. Most states cap rates at levels that make payday-style lending unprofitable.

industries.industry: Banks and fintech lenders using 'rent-a-bank' partnerships
industries.note: The bill closes the loophole by which nonbank lenders originate high-rate loans through a partner bank chartered in a state with no rate cap. Banks doing ordinary-rate lending would see little change.
